title: Linux from Scratch: The Shell, Files, Permissions and Servers
subtitle: A hands-on tour of the Linux command line, with a working Linux-like shell in every lab
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A condensed, original course on using and administering Linux. It covers the filesystem tree, the shell and its commands, files and directories, redirection and pipes, text tools, permissions and ownership, users and sudo, processes and signals, packages and services, shell scripting, networking basics, disks, logs and cron, security basics, and a capstone where you fix a broken server. Every shell lab runs a Linux-like simulator inside the app, built on the Jade Agent Kit virtual filesystem, with real BusyBox WebAssembly tools for grep, sed, awk and sort. It is a teaching sandbox, not a full Linux: some commands are simulated. Credits: BusyBox (GPL-2.0) and the Jade Agent Kit (MIT).

chapters.title: What Linux is
summary: Linux is a kernel, the core program that talks to the hardware and shares it between programs. Around it sits a set of tools, and the bundle is called a distribution, such as Debian, Ubuntu or Fedora.
Everything is organised as one tree of files starting at a single root called slash. Devices, settings and even running processes appear as files in that tree.
You will work in a terminal and a shell, because that is how servers, containers and cloud machines are run.

glossary.def: The core of the operating system. It schedules programs, manages memory and drives hardware.
A kernel plus tools, an installer and a package manager, ready to use.
A program that reads your commands and runs them. Bash is the most common.
Two things: the top directory /, and the all-powerful administrator account.

keyPoints: Linux is the kernel; a distribution is the complete system.
One tree of files starts at /.
Almost everything is a file or behaves like one.
Servers, phones, routers and clouds mostly run Linux.

items: ELI5. Linux is the engine of a car. A distribution is the whole car: engine, seats and steering wheel, ready to drive. The files live in one big tree with a single root.

Linux started in 1991 as a kernel written by Linus Torvalds and grew through thousands of contributors. The kernel decides which program runs when, hands out memory, and talks to disks, networks and screens. It does not include a text editor or a shell.
Those come from other projects, and a distribution packages them together.

Distributions differ in tools and defaults, but they share the same kernel ideas and nearly the same commands. Debian and Ubuntu use the apt package manager. Fedora and Red Hat use dnf. Alpine is tiny and popular in containers. Learn the common core and you can work on all of them.

Linux has one filesystem tree. There are no drive letters. A second disk is attached at a directory, called mounting. Programs live under /usr and /bin, settings under /etc, your files under /home, logs under /var/log, temporary files under /tmp.
Special files in /dev stand for devices, and /proc shows live information about running processes.

lesson.code:
/            the root of everything
├── bin       essential commands
├── etc       configuration files
├── home      one directory per user
│   └── user
├── tmp       temporary files, cleared on reboot
├── usr       installed programs and libraries
└── var       data that changes: logs, caches, mail

items: The idea that many things are files is powerful. You can read a device, search a log or redirect output with the same few tools. In the lab at the end of the next chapter you will move around a small Linux-like machine that runs right inside this app.

chapters.title: The shell and your first commands
summary: The shell shows a prompt and waits. You type a command, possibly with options and arguments, and press Enter. The shell finds the program, runs it and prints the result.
Start with five commands: pwd says where you are, ls lists what is here, cd moves, cat shows a file, and man or --help explains anything.
Tab completes names and the up arrow recalls earlier lines, which saves a lot of typing.

glossary.def: A program or built-in the shell runs, such as ls.
A flag that changes behaviour, such as -l, usually starting with a dash.
What the command works on, such as a file name.
The directory the shell is currently in.
The location of a file, absolute from / or relative to here.

keyPoints: A command line is command, options, arguments.
Absolute paths start with /; relative paths do not.
. is here, .. is the parent, ~ is your home.
Tab completes and history recalls.

items: ELI5. The shell is a text chat with your computer. You type a short order like ls, press Enter, and it answers. Tab finishes the word for you.

A command line has a simple shape: the command name, then options, then arguments. In ls -l /etc the command is ls, the option is -l, which means long listing, and the argument is the directory /etc. Options can usually be combined, so ls -la means long listing including hidden files.

A path names a file. An absolute path starts at the root and works from anywhere, like /home/user/notes.txt. A relative path starts at the working directory, like docs/a.md. Two dots mean the parent directory, one dot means here, and a tilde means your home directory.
Files whose names start with a dot are hidden from a plain ls.

lesson.code:
pwd              # print working directory
ls               # list names
ls -la           # long, including hidden files
cd docs          # move into docs
cd ..            # up one level
cd               # home
cat notes.txt    # print a file
man ls           # the manual page

items: The prompt usually shows your user, the machine and the directory, and ends with a dollar sign for a normal user or a hash for root. Press Tab to complete a name, press it twice to see the choices, and use the up arrow to recall a previous command.

chapters.title: Files and directories
summary: You create, copy, move and delete with a small set of commands. mkdir makes directories, touch makes an empty file, cp copies, mv moves or renames, and rm removes.
Deleting is permanent: there is no recycle bin on the command line. Use rm -r for directories and think before you press Enter.
Wildcards let one pattern name many files, and find searches by name, type and more.

glossary.def: A pattern character the shell expands: * matches any text, ? matches one character.
Applied to a directory and everything inside it, usually with -r.
The record that stores a file's size, owner, permissions and where its data is.
A small file that points to another path.

keyPoints: mkdir -p makes parent directories too.
mv is also rename.
rm is permanent; rm -r removes directories.
* matches any characters, ? matches one.

items: ELI5. Files are like paper in folders. mkdir builds a folder, cp makes a copy, mv moves or renames, and rm puts it in the shredder. There is no bin to dig it out of.

To make a directory, use mkdir. With -p it creates the whole chain, so mkdir -p project/src/app works even if project does not exist yet. To make an empty file, use touch, which also updates the modified time of a file that already exists.

cp copies a file, and cp -r copies a directory with everything in it. mv moves a file to a new place, and because moving within a directory just changes the name, mv is also the rename command. rm deletes. There is no undo, so rm -r on the wrong directory is a classic disaster.
Never run rm -rf with a variable you have not checked.

lesson.code:
mkdir -p project/src
touch project/src/main.txt
cp project/src/main.txt project/backup.txt
mv project/backup.txt project/old.txt
rm project/old.txt
ls project/*.txt            # wildcard
find project -name '*.txt'  # search by name

items: Wildcards are expanded by the shell before the command runs. If a directory holds a.txt, b.txt and notes.md, the pattern *.txt becomes a.txt b.txt. Quote a pattern when you want the command, not the shell, to see it, as with find -name '*.txt'.

chapters.title: Viewing, searching and redirecting
summary: Every program has three streams: standard input, standard output and standard error. By default they connect to the terminal, but you can redirect them.
> sends output to a file and replaces it, >> appends, < feeds a file in, and 2> catches errors. This turns commands into building blocks.
To look at files, use cat for short ones, head and tail for the ends, less to page, and grep to find lines.

glossary.def: Standard input, stream 0: where a program reads from.
Standard output, stream 1: where normal results go.
Standard error, stream 2: where error messages go.
Pointing a stream at a file instead of the terminal.

keyPoints: > replaces, >> appends.
2> redirects errors; 2>&1 merges them.
head and tail show the ends of a file.
grep prints lines that match.

items: ELI5. Output normally goes to the screen like a talking parrot. A greater-than sign tells the parrot to write on paper instead. Two of them add to the paper.

A program reads from standard input and writes to standard output. Errors go to a separate stream, standard error, so they do not get mixed into results. Both usually show on your screen, which hides the difference until you redirect.

lesson.code:
echo hello > greeting.txt      # create or replace
echo again >> greeting.txt       # append
cat greeting.txt
ls /nope 2> errors.txt           # only errors go to the file
ls /nope /etc > out.txt 2>&1     # both streams into one file
sort < names.txt                  # feed a file as input
ls /nope 2> /dev/null            # throw errors away

items: /dev/null is a special file that discards everything written to it. It is the standard way to silence output you do not need.
To read files: cat prints a whole file, head -n 3 prints the first three lines, tail -n 3 prints the last three, and tail -f follows a log as it grows. less pages through a large file.
grep pattern file prints matching lines; -i ignores case, -n shows line numbers, -v inverts, -c counts and -r searches a directory tree.

chapters.title: Pipes and text tools
summary: A pipe, written |, sends the output of one command into the input of the next. Small tools that each do one thing combine into powerful one-line programs.
The core toolbox: grep to filter, sort to order, uniq -c to count repeats, wc to count, cut and awk to pick columns, sed to edit streams and tr to translate characters.
A classic pipeline counts something in a log: filter with grep, take a column, sort, count with uniq -c, sort again.

glossary.def: The | operator: output of the left command becomes input of the right.
A program that reads a stream and writes a changed stream.
A pattern language for matching text, used by grep, sed and awk.
A column of a line, separated by spaces or another delimiter.

keyPoints: cmd1 | cmd2 feeds output to input.
sort | uniq -c counts repeats; uniq needs sorted input.
awk '{print $1}' prints the first column.
sed 's/old/new/' replaces text.

items: ELI5. A pipe is a slide between two helpers. One helper finds the red blocks, slides them to the next who sorts them, and the last one counts how many.
The Unix idea is small tools that do one job and work together. A pipe joins them. Because everything is text, any tool can read what another wrote, with no special format.

lesson.code:
# which pages are visited most?
cat access.log | awk '{print $3}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3

# count lines that mention ERROR
grep -c ERROR app.log

# replace text in a stream
echo 'hello world' | sed 's/world/Linux/'

# first and fifth fields of the passwd file
cut -d: -f1,5 /etc/passwd

items: uniq only collapses neighbouring duplicates, which is why you nearly always sort first. sort -n sorts numerically, -r reverses, and -k picks a column. wc -l counts lines, wc -w words. tr a-z A-Z turns lowercase into uppercase. xargs turns lines of input into arguments of another command.
awk treats each line as fields named $1, $2 and so on, and $0 is the whole line. awk '{print $2}' prints the second column. awk '$4 == 404' prints lines whose fourth field is 404.
sed handles replacements and deletions: sed 's/a/b/g' replaces every a, and sed '/debug/d' deletes lines containing debug.

chapters.title: Permissions and ownership

maps.title: Permissions
links: Group | is | A set of users

summary: Every file has an owner, a group and three sets of permission bits: for the owner, for the group and for everyone else. Each set can allow read, write and execute.
ls -l shows them as ten characters like -rwxr-xr--. chmod changes them with numbers, such as 755, or letters, such as u+x.
Permissions on a directory mean something different: read lists names, write adds or removes entries, execute lets you enter.

glossary.def: The permission bits of a file.
Base 8: one digit per set, r=4, w=2, x=1 added together.
A mask that removes permissions from newly created files.
A bit that makes a program run with its owner's rights.

keyPoints: r=4, w=2, x=1; add them per set.
755 is rwxr-xr-x, 644 is rw-r--r--.
Directories need x to be entered.
umask 022 gives files 644 and directories 755.

items: ELI5. Every file has a little lock card: who the owner is, who the team is and what everyone else may do. Read, write, run are worth four, two and one points.

A line from ls -l reads like this: -rwxr-xr-- 1 alice dev 120 Nov 9 10:00 run.sh. The first character is the type, a dash for a file and d for a directory. Then come three triples for the owner, the group and others. Then the link count, the owner, the group, the size, the date and the name.

lesson.code:
-rwxr-xr--   owner can read, write, execute
                group can read, execute
                others can only read

r = 4   w = 2   x = 1
rwx = 7   r-x = 5   r-- = 4   so this mode is 754

items: chmod accepts a number or a symbolic expression. chmod 644 notes.txt sets rw-r--r--. chmod u+x run.sh adds execute for the owner. chmod go-w file removes write from group and others. chmod -R applies to a whole tree.
Only the owner or root can change a file's mode, and only root can change its owner with chown.

For directories: read lets you list the names, write lets you create or delete entries inside, and execute lets you cd into it and reach the files inside. A directory with mode 700 is private to its owner.
The sticky bit on /tmp stops users from deleting each other's files even though everyone can write there.
New files get 666 for files and 777 for directories, minus the umask. With the usual umask 022, files come out 644 and directories 755. A umask of 077 makes everything private.

practice.title: Octal to permission string
practice.intro: Write octal_to_perm(o) that turns '640' into 'rw-r-----'.
practice.hint: For each digit test the 4, 2 and 1 bits.
practice.solution:
def octal_to_perm(o):
    out = ''
    for d in o:
        n = int(d)
        out += 'r' if n >= 4 else '-'
        out += 'w' if n % 4 >= 2 else '-'
        out += 'x' if n % 2 == 1 else '-'
    return out

chapters.title: Users, groups and sudo
summary: Every process and file belongs to a user and a group. A user is a number, the UID, with a name; root is UID 0 and may do anything.
Day to day you work as a normal user and borrow root's power only when needed, with sudo, which asks for your password and logs what you ran.
Users and groups live in plain text files under /etc, and a handful of commands manage them: useradd, usermod, groupadd, passwd, id and groups.

glossary.def: The numeric id of a user. Root is 0; normal users usually start at 1000.
The numeric id of a group.
Runs one command with another user's rights, normally root's, if you are allowed.
The configuration that says who may use sudo.

keyPoints: id shows your uid, gid and groups.
Work as a normal user; use sudo only when needed.
usermod -aG adds a user to a group; forget -a and you replace the groups.
/etc/passwd has seven colon-separated fields.

items: ELI5. Users are the people with keys. Root has a master key to everything. sudo is like asking the grown-up to open one door for you and writing it in a diary.

Linux decides what you may do by your user id and group ids. The names are only labels; the kernel works with numbers. The id command shows both. A user can belong to many groups, which is how you share a project directory: put the team in one group and give that group write access.

lesson.code:
# /etc/passwd: name : x : uid : gid : comment : home : shell
alice:x:1001:1001:Alice:/home/alice:/bin/bash

id                       # uid=1000(user) gid=1000(user) groups=...
sudo useradd -m zed      # make a user and a home directory
sudo usermod -aG dev zed # add zed to the group dev
sudo passwd zed          # set a password
sudo -u alice ls /home/alice   # run one command as alice

items: Root can read every file, kill any process and change any setting, so a typo as root can destroy a machine. That is why servers disable direct root logins and rely on sudo. Members of the sudo group, or of wheel on some distributions, may use it. Each use is written to the log.

Be careful with usermod. The option -aG appends to the supplementary groups. Without -a the user's groups are replaced by exactly the list you gave, which can lock someone out of the sudo group by accident.

chapters.title: Processes, jobs and signals
summary: A process is a running program with its own number, the PID, an owner and its own memory. The first process, init or systemd, is PID 1 and starts the rest.
ps shows a snapshot, top shows it live. kill does not just kill: it sends a signal. SIGTERM, the default, asks politely; SIGKILL cannot be ignored.
Add & to run a command in the background so you keep your prompt.

glossary.def: Process id: the number the kernel uses to name a running program.
A small message sent to a process, such as TERM or KILL.
A background process that provides a service.
A finished process whose parent has not yet collected its exit status.

keyPoints: ps aux lists all processes.
kill sends TERM (15) by default; kill -9 sends KILL.
A trailing & runs a command in the background.
Exit code 0 means success.

items: ELI5. A process is a worker doing a job with a name tag number. You can ask it to stop nicely, or, if it will not listen, pull the plug.

Every command you run becomes a process. The kernel gives it a PID and records who started it, which is its owner. A process can start children. Your shell is the parent of the commands you type. When a parent ends, its children are adopted by PID 1.

lesson.code:
ps                 # your own processes
ps aux             # every process, with owner and CPU use
ps -ef | grep ssh  # find one by name
top                # live view
sleep 300 &        # run in the background
jobs               # background jobs of this shell
kill 1234          # ask process 1234 to stop (TERM)
kill -9 1234       # force it (KILL)

items: Signals are numbered messages. 15 is TERM, a polite request that lets the program clean up. 2 is INT, what Ctrl+C sends. 1 is HUP, often used to make a daemon reload its settings. 9 is KILL, which the kernel carries out immediately and no program can catch, so it gives no chance to save work.
Try TERM first, and use KILL only when a process refuses to stop.

You may only signal your own processes unless you are root. Every command also ends with an exit code, a number that the shell keeps in the variable $?. Zero means success and anything else means failure. Scripts and pipelines use this to decide what to do next.

chapters.title: Packages and services
summary: A package manager installs software, resolves what it depends on, and keeps it updated from trusted repositories. On Debian and Ubuntu that is apt.
A service is a program that runs in the background, such as a web server. systemd starts services at boot and systemctl controls them.
The pattern is always the same: install the package, start the service, enable it for boot, check its status and read its logs.

glossary.def: A bundle of files plus metadata such as version and dependencies.
A server that holds signed packages.
The init system that boots the machine and supervises services.
A thing systemd manages, such as nginx.service.

keyPoints: sudo apt update refreshes the list; apt install adds a package.
systemctl start, stop, restart, status control a service.
enable makes it start at boot; start runs it now.
journalctl -u name reads its log.

items: ELI5. An app store for grown-up computers: apt fetches a program and everything it needs. A service is a worker who stays at the shop all day, and systemctl is the boss.

On Debian-style systems, apt update downloads the list of what is available, apt install name installs it and everything it needs, apt remove deletes it, and apt search finds names. All of these except search need root, so you write sudo in front.
Packages are signed, so a repository cannot slip you something altered.

lesson.code:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install nginx
systemctl status nginx          # is it running?
sudo systemctl start nginx      # run it now
sudo systemctl enable nginx     # and at every boot
sudo systemctl restart nginx    # after changing its config
journalctl -u nginx -n 20       # the last 20 log lines

items: systemd reads small unit files that say what to run, what it needs and when to restart it. Start means run now, enable means run at boot, and they are separate. A service can be enabled but stopped, or running but not enabled. After editing a unit file, run systemctl daemon-reload.
Other families use other tools with the same ideas: dnf or yum on Fedora and Red Hat, apk on Alpine, pacman on Arch. Learning one makes the others easy.

links: Script | is | A text file of commands
Exit code | reports | Success or failure

summary: A shell script is a text file of commands. Start it with a shebang line like #!/bin/bash, make it executable with chmod +x, and run it with ./script.sh.
Variables hold text. Assign with name=value, no spaces, and read with $name. Arguments arrive as $1, $2 and so on, and $# is how many there are.
if tests a condition, usually with [ ] and operators such as -f for file exists, -eq for equal numbers and = for equal text.

glossary.def: The first line #! followed by the interpreter, like #!/bin/bash.
A named piece of text. You set it with name=value and read it with $name.
A value passed on the command line, available as $1, $2, ...
The [ ] command, which succeeds or fails depending on a condition.

keyPoints: No spaces around = in an assignment.
Quote variables: "$name".
[ -f file ] tests that a file exists.
$? holds the last exit code.

items: ELI5. A script is a recipe card with commands instead of steps. The first line says who should read it, and a plus-x sticker lets it run on its own.

A script is just commands you would otherwise type. Put #!/bin/bash on the first line so the system knows which interpreter to use, save the file, run chmod +x on it and start it with ./name.sh. The dot-slash is needed because the current directory is normally not on your command search path.

lesson.code:
#!/bin/bash
# greet.sh: say hello
name="$1"
if [ -z "$name" ]; then
  echo "usage: $0 NAME"
  exit 1
fi
echo "Hello, $name!"
echo "You gave $# argument(s)"

items: Variables have no spaces around the equals sign: name=Lilith works, name = Lilith does not. Always put double quotes around a variable when you use it, so that a value with spaces stays one word. Single quotes stop all expansion. $(command) captures a command's output, as in today=$(date).

The test command, written [ ], returns success or failure. Useful tests: -f is a regular file, -d is a directory, -e exists, -z string empty, -n string not empty, = and != compare text, -eq -ne -lt -gt compare numbers. Combine with && for and, and || for or.
Every command sets an exit code, readable as $?, and if looks at it.

chapters.title: Shell scripting II: loops, functions and robustness

maps.title: Loops
links: while | repeats while | A test is true

summary: for repeats a block for each item in a list, while repeats as long as a test succeeds. Functions give a name to a group of commands.
Scripts should fail loudly. set -e stops the script at the first failing command, and checking exit codes lets you react to problems.
Small, tested scripts are the glue of system administration: backups, deployments, reports and clean-up jobs.

glossary.def: A construct that repeats commands.
A named group of commands you can call like a command.
A wildcard pattern such as *.log, expanded by the shell.
Safe to run twice: the second run changes nothing.

keyPoints: for x in list; do ...; done.
while test; do ...; done.
set -e stops at the first error.
Write idempotent scripts: mkdir -p, not mkdir.

items: ELI5. Loops are a rule like: do this for every apple in the basket. A function is a recipe you give a name to so you can call it any time.

lesson.code:
# for loop over files
for f in *.txt; do
  echo "checking $f"
  wc -l "$f"
done

# counting loop
i=1
while [ $i -le 3 ]; do
  echo "round $i"
  i=$((i + 1))
done

# a function
backup() {
  cp "$1" "$1.bak"
  echo "saved $1"
}
backup notes.txt

items: The for loop walks a list: words, file names from a wildcard, or numbers from seq. The while loop repeats while its test succeeds. Inside a loop, break leaves the loop and continue skips to the next round. Arithmetic uses double parentheses: $((i + 1)).
A function takes its own arguments as $1, $2, and returns an exit code with return. case matches a value against patterns and is tidier than a chain of ifs when you check an option or an extension.

Robust scripts check their work. Put set -e near the top so a failure stops the script instead of letting it plough on. Test that a file exists before reading it. Quote everything. Make scripts idempotent: use mkdir -p, ln -sf and cp -u so running them again is harmless.
Print what you are doing so a log shows where it failed.

chapters.title: Networking basics
summary: Every machine on a network has an IP address. A port number picks the program on that machine, so a web server listens on 80 or 443 and SSH on 22.
DNS turns names such as example.com into addresses. A subnet like 192.168.1.0/24 describes a block of addresses that share a prefix.
Learn four tools: ip addr to see your address, ping to test reachability, curl to talk to web services, and ss to see what is listening.

glossary.def: A number that identifies a network interface, like 192.168.1.23.
A number from 0 to 65535 that picks a service on a host.
The system that maps names to addresses.
Notation like /24 saying how many leading bits form the network part.

keyPoints: 22 is SSH, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 53 DNS.
/24 means the first 24 bits are the network.
ping tests reachability; curl tests a service.
ss -tln shows listening TCP ports.

items: ELI5. Every computer has a house number, called an IP address, and every program has a door number called a port. A web server waits at door 80.

An IPv4 address is four numbers from 0 to 255, such as 192.168.1.23. Those are 32 bits. A slash number says how many leading bits name the network. A /24 network has 256 addresses that share the first three numbers.
Private ranges such as 192.168.0.0/16, 10.0.0.0/8 and 172.16.0.0/12 are not routed on the internet.

lesson.code:
ip addr              # my addresses
ping -c 2 localhost  # is it reachable?
curl http://localhost    # fetch a page
ss -tln              # which TCP ports are listening
curl -I https://example.com   # headers only

items: A connection needs an address and a port. The same machine can run SSH on 22 and a web server on 80 at once. When a service is down, curl says connection refused. When a name does not resolve, it says could not resolve host. Those two messages point to different problems: the service or the DNS.

To work on remote machines you use SSH, a secure shell. ssh user@host logs in, and key pairs are safer than passwords. scp and rsync copy files over it. This sandbox is offline, so ssh is not available here, but the commands are the same on a real server.

chapters.title: Disks, logs and scheduled jobs

maps.title: Disks
links: cron | runs | Jobs on a schedule

summary: Disks are split into partitions, each with a filesystem, and each mounted at a directory. df shows free space for every mount and du shows how much a directory uses.
Logs under /var/log and in the journal are where machines explain themselves. The first question when something breaks is: what does the log say?
cron runs commands on a schedule written as five time fields.

glossary.def: Attach a filesystem to a directory so its files appear in the tree.
A section of a disk that holds a filesystem.
A file or stream of timestamped messages about what a program did.
The scheduler that runs commands at set times.

keyPoints: df -h shows free space; du -sh shows a directory's size.
Full disks are a very common failure.
crontab fields: minute hour day month weekday.
*/5 means every five.

items: ELI5. Disks are shelves that fill up. Logs are a diary the computer writes about itself. Cron is an alarm clock that starts jobs at the times you set.

df -h lists every mounted filesystem with its size, used space and free space in human units. du -sh dir tells you how big one directory is, and du -sh * | sort -h shows which items are largest. A full disk breaks databases and logging, so checking df is a reflex.

lesson.code:
df -h                          # free space per mount
du -sh /var/log                # size of one directory
ls -lh /var/log                # sizes in human units
tail -n 20 /var/log/syslog     # the last 20 messages
journalctl -n 20               # same, from systemd
grep -i error /var/log/syslog | tail -5

items: A crontab line has five time fields and then a command: minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week. A star means every value, a comma lists values, a dash gives a range and a slash gives a step. So */15 * * * * runs every 15 minutes and 30 2 * * 1 runs at 02:30 every Monday.
Edit your table with crontab -e and show it with crontab -l.

lesson.code:
# m  h  dom mon dow  command
*/15 *  *   *   *    /home/user/check.sh
30   2  *   *   1    /home/user/backup.sh
0    9  1   *   *    echo monthly report

items: Logs grow without limit, so logrotate renames and compresses old ones on a schedule. The /etc/fstab file lists the filesystems to mount at boot; a typo there can stop a machine from booting, so take care and keep a copy.

chapters.title: Security basics
summary: Security is a habit of small controls: give every user and program only the access it needs, keep software updated, use keys instead of passwords, and close ports you do not use.
On a server, the usual first steps are to disable root login over SSH, disable password logins, turn on a firewall and set up automatic security updates.
Assume something will fail anyway. Logs help you notice and backups help you recover.

glossary.def: Giving each user and program only the access needed.
A filter that allows or blocks network traffic by rule.
A pair of files: a private key you keep and a public key you put on the server.
Reducing the ways a system can be attacked.

keyPoints: Disable root and password SSH logins.
Open only the ports you need.
Apply security updates promptly.
Test your backups by restoring one.

items: ELI5. Security is locking doors. Use a key instead of a password, only open the doors you need, keep the locks updated and keep a spare copy of your treasures somewhere else.

Start from least privilege. Files should be readable only by those who need them, services should run as their own unprivileged users and administrators should use sudo so that actions are logged. Never make a file world-writable to cure a permissions error.
Find out which user and group actually need access and grant just that.

lesson.code:
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config: the lines that matter
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
PubkeyAuthentication yes

sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp
sudo ufw enable

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

items: Passwords can be guessed by bots, and servers see thousands of attempts a day. SSH keys cannot be guessed: you hold the private key and the server holds the public one. Turn off password logins once your key works.
A firewall then makes sure that only the ports you chose, such as 22, 80 and 443, answer at all.

Watch for trouble in the logs. Many failed logins from one address, a user you did not create, or a program running from /tmp are all warnings. And keep backups somewhere else, because a backup on the same disk fails along with it. A backup is only real after you have restored from it once.

chapters.title: Capstone: look after a small server
summary: Put everything together. You are handed a small server with a few problems. Look around, install and start the web service, fix risky permissions, add a teammate and check your work.
Work like a system administrator: inspect first, change one thing at a time and verify each change before moving on.
When the checklist is complete you will have used navigation, files, permissions, users, packages, services and scripting on one machine.

glossary.def: A written list of steps for a routine or emergency task.
Check that a change did what you intended.
Known good state to compare against.
A review of what exists and who may do what.

keyPoints: Look before you change.
Change one thing and verify it.
Keep scripts and notes of what you did.
Prefer reversible changes.

items: ELI5. Be a computer doctor: look first, change one thing, check it worked. Then write down what you did so the next person can follow your steps.

A good administrator works in a loop: observe, change, verify. Start by finding out what you have: who you are, what is running, how much space is free and what the logs say. Then fix the most urgent problem first, and check that it worked.

In the lab below you will find a web root with files that are too open, a missing web server, a runaway process and a teammate who needs access to a shared folder. The checklist tells you what the finished system should look like but not how to get there.
Use the earlier chapters and the Hint button if you get stuck.

Congratulations on getting this far. The skills here carry straight over to real servers, containers and cloud machines, which are almost all Linux. The DevOps course builds on them with version control, pipelines, containers and monitoring.
